entries.claim: Atmosphère 1.12.1 supports firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Firmware compatibility only; not entry-point compatibility.
entries.evidence: The 1.12.1 release notes add support for 23.0.0 and describe the 23.0.0 changes. The maintained NH Switch Guide compatibility checker lists Atmosphère 1.12.1 as supporting firmware 23.0.1. A community reply in Atmosphère issue #2883 also states that the latest release supports 23.0.1.
entries.limitations: The release notes explicitly name 23.0.0; 23.0.1 support is established by the maintained guide and issue discussion. Firmware support does not imply that an entry point exists on Mariko.

entries.claim: hekate v6.5.4 supports Horizon OS 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Bootloader and firmware compatibility only.
entries.evidence: The v6.5.4 release body states: Latest HOS supported: 23.0.1. The release was published 2026-09-28 from commit 45cd81ed08e30a26ba380958c7e20b55c342834b.
entries.limitations: This establishes firmware support, not that the bootloader can be launched on an unmodified OLED.

entries.claim: The Nintendo Switch OLED (model HEG-001) uses a Mariko/Tegra X1+ SoC on an ODNX10-A1 motherboard.
entries.scope: Hardware identification.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's hardware page lists the OLED motherboard as ODNX10-A1 and identifies the OLED SoC family as Tegra X1+ / Mariko. Nintendo's support page lists the OLED model number as HEG-001.
entries.limitations: The user's specific console has not been opened or independently identified. The owner manually confirmed the model and firmware on 2026-10-26, but that confirmation is owner-reported and not independently observed.

entries.claim: CVE-2018-6242 (Fusée Gelée) is a Tegra BootROM Recovery Mode buffer overflow affecting Tegra mobile processors released before 2016.
entries.scope: Vulnerability description.
entries.evidence: The NVD record states that some NVIDIA Tegra mobile processors released prior to 2016 contain a buffer overflow in BootROM Recovery Mode (RCM), exploitable with physical USB access and the ability to force RCM.
entries.limitations: The NVD record describes the vulnerability class and affected generation; it does not by itself prove which later hardware revisions are patched. The Mariko conclusion is supported separately by E-005 and E-006.

entries.claim: Patched and Mariko consoles can enter RCM, but cannot receive a payload over RCM.
entries.scope: Entry-point behavior on patched/Mariko hardware.
entries.evidence: The NH Switch Guide's Entering RCM page states: Patched units can enter RCM, but it is not possible to send a payload on those systems.
entries.limitations: The guide is maintained community documentation, not a Nintendo statement. The behavior is consistent with the patched bootROM described by the same guide.

entries.claim: The maintained NH Switch Guide routes patched and Mariko consoles to a modchip rather than a software-only entry point.
entries.scope: Documented public guidance.
entries.evidence: The guide states that patched consoles are immune to the fusee-gelee exploit in RCM, that attempting to inject a payload on a patched console will be unsuccessful, and that modchips allow any patched console to run CFW. Its firmware table maps patched/Mariko consoles on 5.0.0 or later to the modchip route.
entries.limitations: This is evidence about documented guidance, not a mathematical proof that no software-only method can ever exist.

entries.claim: A publicly documented, reproducible software-only entry point to Atmosphère exists for an unmodified Switch OLED on firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Reviewed public documentation as of 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: No reviewed source describes a software-only Mariko/OLED entry point to Atmosphère. The authoritative maintained guide explicitly routes patched/Mariko consoles to a modchip and states that RCM payload injection does not work on them. Atmosphère and hekate document firmware support, not an OLED entry point. The ns2jb write-up reports a software-only userland/sysmodule chain tested on Switch 1, but it is unpackaged, does not provide CFW or kernel access, and is not shown on OLED/23.0.1 (E-022, E-032).
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding, not proof that no undisclosed exploit exists. It does not deny that a userland/sysmodule chain exists; it denies that a public chain to Atmosphère on the target exists. The search was limited to public documentation and releases reviewed on 2026-10-26; it was not an exhaustive audit of private research.

entries.claim: The documented route to Atmosphère on an unmodified OLED is a hardware modchip, which is outside this project's software-only scope.
entries.scope: Documented alternative route; not a software-only method.
entries.evidence: The NH Switch Guide describes modchips as a CPU voltage-glitching hardware modification that bypasses bootROM verification and allows a payload to be launched on patched consoles. Installation requires microsoldering.
entries.limitations: This project does not provide installation instructions, tooling, or automation for modchips. Hardware modification carries warranty, safety, and bricking risks.

entries.claim: The target console is a Nintendo Switch OLED (HEG-001) running firmware 23.0.1, with no prior opening or modchip reported.
entries.scope: Target identity; firmware and serial prefix observed via PTP.
entries.evidence: The owner manually confirmed HEG-001, firmware 23.0.1, serial prefix XTJ, and no modification history on 2026-10-26. PTP GetDeviceInfo on the same date reported Device version 23.0.1 and serial prefix XTJ***, with 10 operations and no session. See research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-manual.json and research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-ptp.json.
entries.limitations: PTP confirms what the console reports, not the exact model number (DeviceInfo says 'Nintendo Switch'), OLED-versus-LCD hardware, no-modchip status, integrity, or exploitability. The HEG-001 model number and modification history remain owner-reported.

entries.claim: Switch Capmtp DeviceInfo reports the console serial number and system display version through the standard PTP DeviceInfo fields.
entries.scope: Documented PTP behavior on Switch system firmware 11.0.0 and later.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew states that DeviceInfo Serial Number is set to the output of GetSerialNumber and Device Version is set to SystemVersion DisplayVersion.
entries.limitations: The documentation is reverse-engineered and does not guarantee behavior on every firmware revision. Hardware validation on this OLED is recorded in E-037.

entries.claim: USB product ID 0x057e:0x201d is associated with Nintendo Switch / Switch Lite PTP mode.
entries.scope: USB identification on Switch and Switch Lite.
entries.evidence: libmtp's device table lists Nintendo 0x057e:0x201d as Switch / Switch Lite. The related libmtp issue documents Switch PTP/MTP support added in system firmware 11.0.0.
entries.limitations: The libmtp table does not list the OLED separately; OLED applicability is tracked as E-012.

entries.claim: A Switch OLED in Copy to PC via USB mode enumerates as 0x057e:0x201d and answers PTP GetDeviceInfo.
entries.scope: OLED hardware behavior; observed on the target console.
entries.evidence: On 2026-10-26 the target OLED enumerated as 0x057e:0x201d in Copy to PC via USB mode and answered PTP GetDeviceInfo without opening a session. DeviceInfo reported Manufacturer Nintendo, Model Nintendo Switch, Device version 23.0.1, serial prefix XTJ***, and 10 operations. See research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-ptp.json.
entries.limitations: PTP DeviceInfo is what the console reports; modified firmware could spoof it. The model string is generic and does not distinguish OLED from LCD. This is one console and one observation, not a general OLED compatibility proof.

entries.claim: USB product ID 0x057e:0x2061 is associated with Nintendo Switch 2 PTP mode.
entries.scope: USB identification; not the target model.
entries.evidence: libmtp's device table lists Nintendo 0x057e:0x2061 as Switch 2. The libmtp issue shows a Switch 2 PTP DeviceInfo response with model, device version, serial number, and the nintendo.com: 1.0 vendor extension.
entries.limitations: The Switch 2 is a different console and must not be confused with the OLED target.

entries.claim: USB product ID 0x0955:0x7321 is the NVIDIA Tegra APX / Switch RCM identity.
entries.scope: USB identification of RCM/APX mode.
entries.evidence: TegraRcmSmash documents default USB IDs 0x0955:0x7321 for a Switch in RCM mode. The tool is listed for identification only; this project does not send payloads.
entries.limitations: Enumeration in RCM does not prove that a payload can be accepted. On patched/Mariko hardware it cannot be.

entries.claim: Stock Switch USB PTP mode exposes only PTP operations 0x1001-0x100A and does not expose a shell, ADB, or general-purpose remote-control interface.
entries.scope: Documented stock USB surface.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew states that only PTP operations 0x1001-0x100A are available. No reviewed source documents a stock shell, ADB, or general-purpose remote-control interface over USB.
entries.limitations: This describes the documented stock interface. It does not rule out vendor-specific or undisclosed behavior.

entries.claim: An undisclosed software-only exploit exists for Mariko/OLED on firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Non-public vulnerability research.
entries.evidence: No public evidence was found in the reviewed sources. This claim cannot be tested from public documentation or from the console's stock USB interface.
entries.limitations: Private research may exist. This ledger does not claim that a software-only method is impossible, only that no qualifying public method was verified.

entries.claim: Firmware compatibility with Atmosphère and hekate does not establish that an entry point exists on Mariko/OLED hardware.
entries.scope: Analytical distinction between firmware support and exploit compatibility.
entries.evidence: Atmosphère and hekate document support for the firmware's system modules and boot process. The NH Switch Guide separately documents that patched/Mariko consoles cannot receive an RCM payload and require a modchip. These are independent axes.
entries.limitations: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited sources; it does not add new hardware evidence.

entries.claim: PTP GetDeviceInfo is a read-only identity query and does not prove boot state, exploitability, or CFW access.
entries.scope: Protocol capability and limits.
entries.evidence: PTP operation 0x1001 returns a DeviceInfo dataset. The dataset contains identity and capability fields such as manufacturer, model, device version, serial number, and supported operations. It does not execute code or report boot state.
entries.limitations: A device response can be spoofed by modified firmware; this project treats PTP output as an observation, not proof of console integrity.

entries.claim: USB product ID 0x057e:0x2000 is associated with Nintendo Switch normal USB mode.
entries.scope: USB identification; vendor database only.
entries.evidence: DeviceHunt lists Nintendo 0x057e:0x2000 as Switch.
entries.limitations: This is a third-party device database, not protocol documentation. The tool reports it as a recognizable Nintendo device but does not claim any control capability.

entries.claim: USB product ID 0x057e:0x2009 is associated with the Nintendo Switch Pro Controller.
entries.scope: USB identification; not a console.
entries.evidence: DeviceHunt lists Nintendo 0x057e:0x2009 as Switch Pro Controller.
entries.limitations: This is a third-party device database. The tool classifies it as a controller, not a console.

entries.claim: ns2jb is a software-only, tethered userland/sysmodule jailbreak for the Nintendo Switch 2 on system software 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Switch 2 only; userland/sysmodule code execution.
entries.evidence: The author's write-up states that ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2 on 23.0.1, running arbitrary native code as ordinary sysmodules and as the built-in fs sysmodule. The repository README states 'Switch 2 only' and that the demo does not install custom firmware or persistence.
entries.limitations: This is not the OLED target. It does not provide kernel access, bootROM access, or custom firmware. It requires SmileBASIC 4.4.9 and a host on the same network.

entries.claim: The ns2jb exploit chain was also tested on a Switch 1, but it has not been packaged for Switch 1 and does not provide modchip-level capability.
entries.scope: Author-reported Switch 1 test; not a release.
entries.evidence: The write-up states: 'The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.'
entries.limitations: The write-up does not identify the Switch 1 model, firmware version, or whether it was an OLED/Mariko unit. 'Tested' is not a reproducible package. The published repository is Switch 2 only. This does not establish a path to Atmosphère, kernel, or bootROM.

entries.claim: CVE-2026-82079 is a stack-based buffer overflow in Nintendo Switch local wireless networking that affects system versions before 23.0.0 and is fixed in 23.0.0.
entries.scope: Vulnerability description and fixed version.
entries.evidence: The CVE record lists CWE-121, an adjacent-network attack vector, CVSS 4.0 base score 7.0, affected versions before 23.0.0, and a solution of system update 23.0.0. Switchbrew 23.0.0 states that an ldn vulnerability was fixed (CVE-2026-82079).
entries.limitations: The CVE record describes the vulnerability class and patch; it does not provide exploit code. The target is reported to be on 23.0.1, so this fixed flaw is not available to it.

entries.claim: Switchbrew's 23.0.0 changelog documents fixes for bsdsocket AddrInfo deserialization, multiple audio validation issues, and the ldn CVE.
entries.scope: Documented 23.0.0 security fixes.
entries.evidence: The 23.0.0 page states that a vulnerability was fixed in the nnSdk AddrInfo deserialization code used by bsdsocket; that audio RequestUpdate now performs additional validation and includes vulnerability fixes; and that an ldn vulnerability was fixed (CVE-2026-82079). The flaw list marks the corresponding entries fixed in 23.0.0.
entries.limitations: This is a public changelog and flaw list, not a complete audit of 23.0.1. It does not prove that no other flaw exists.

entries.claim: Switchbrew's 23.0.1 page documents a stability fix and an sdb/SystemVersion update, and does not list a security fix.
entries.scope: Documented 23.0.1 changes.
entries.evidence: The page states that 23.0.1 fixed an issue from 23.0.0 where software occasionally took a long time to start, pause, or close. It lists sdb as the only updated sysmodule and SystemVersion as updated. Its security-flaw field is the unfilled wiki placeholder 'Security flaws fixed: <fill this in manually>'.
entries.limitations: The placeholder means the wiki page is incomplete. The absence of a listed security fix is not proof that 23.0.1 contains none; the official change-log describes a stability update.

entries.claim: PegaSwitch is an archived early-Switch browser exploit toolkit whose documented launch paths target firmware 1.0.0 and the Fake News entry point, not 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Historical browser entry point.
entries.evidence: The archived PegaSwitch README instructs users to start with --webapplet if on 1.0.0 or using the Fake News entry point, and to use a JPN copy of Puyo Puyo Tetris on 1.0.0. The repository was archived on 2021-09-21. Switchbrew documents the WebKit-based browser applets but no 23.0.1 exploit chain.
entries.limitations: The README does not state a hard upper firmware bound. The finding is that its documented paths are for early firmware and it is archived, not that it never worked on any later version. No 23.0.1 support is documented.

entries.claim: Caffeine is an old software exploit for patched Erista consoles on firmware 4.1.0 and does not apply to Mariko/OLED on 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Historical Erista software entry point.
entries.evidence: The NH Switch Guide's compatibility table lists Caffeine for patched systems on 4.1.0 only and states that any firmware version past 4.1.0 is not vulnerable to software exploits.
entries.limitations: The guide is community documentation. It describes the documented route, not a formal proof. Some secondary sources describe the range as 4.0.0-4.1.0; either way, 23.0.1 is far outside it.

entries.claim: A public browser/WebKit exploit chain exists for Switch 1 firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Browser/WebKit entry point on the target firmware.
entries.evidence: No 23.0.1 browser chain is listed in the reviewed flaw list or browser documentation. The ns2jb write-up describes a WebKit attempt on Switch 2 that did not succeed, and a separate SmileBASIC route. No public Switch 1 23.0.1 browser chain was found.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding. Public flaw lists can lag or omit private research. Browser applets remain an attack surface, and the Switch 1 browser environment differs from Switch 2.

entries.claim: The public Bluetooth and local-wireless flaws listed by Switchbrew are fixed before or in 23.0.0, and no public 23.0.1 chain was found.
entries.scope: Bluetooth and local-wireless surfaces on 23.0.1.
entries.evidence: The flaw list marks the listed Bluetooth stack overflows fixed in 15.0.0, 16.0.0, 21.0.0, and 22.0.0, and the ldn flaws fixed in 21.0.0 and 23.0.0. The 23.0.0 page confirms the ldn CVE fix. No public 23.0.1 chain is listed.
entries.limitations: Absence-of-documentation finding. The flaw list is not exhaustive and may not include private research. It does not prove the surfaces are unexploitable.

entries.claim: Recovery/Maintenance mode provides update and format/initialize functions, not an unsigned-code execution path.
entries.scope: Documented recovery-mode behavior.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's Boot Modes page describes Recovery Mode as a menu that allows updating the console through the internet and formatting/initializing it with or without keeping user info, screenshots, and saves. It documents no code execution or payload loading.
entries.limitations: This describes documented stock behavior. It does not rule out a hypothetical vulnerability in the recovery applet, but no public one was found.

entries.claim: The reviewed public flaw list contains no unpatched Mariko software-only boot chain as of 2026-10-26.
entries.scope: Public boot-chain flaws affecting Mariko.
entries.evidence: The flaw list marks the bootROM flaws fixed on Mariko, and lists fixes through 23.0.0 for the reviewed kernel, sysmodule, browser, ldn, and Bluetooth entries. The 23.0.1 page lists only a stability fix. No entry describes an unpatched Mariko boot chain.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding, not proof of impossibility. The list is public and may lag private research. It does not cover every binary or configuration.

entries.claim: The ns2jb userland/sysmodule chain does not provide custom firmware, kernel access, or persistence, and therefore is not a path to Atmosphère by itself.
entries.scope: Capability boundary of the ns2jb chain.
entries.evidence: The write-up states that ns2jb runs native code as ordinary sysmodules and fs, and its conclusion describes the work as a step toward CFW rather than CFW itself. It also says the Switch 1 version 'wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip.' The README states that the demo does not install custom firmware or persistence.
entries.limitations: It could be a stepping stone if combined with additional vulnerabilities; the author says it may help the community make progress toward CFW. It is not a complete chain, and no public kernel or bootROM stage is included.

entries.claim: A publicly documented, reproducible software-only userland-to-bootROM chain exists for the OLED on firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Reviewed public documentation as of 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: No reviewed source connects a userland/sysmodule primitive to kernel or bootROM access on Mariko/OLED. The ns2jb chain stops at sysmodule/fs code execution and explicitly does not provide CFW or kernel access. The maintained NH Switch Guide routes Mariko consoles to a modchip. Atmosphère documents firmware support, not an OLED entry point.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding, not proof that no undisclosed chain exists. The ns2jb Switch 1 test is a lead, but it is unpackaged and its model/firmware are not stated.

entries.claim: The ns2jb chain is confirmed to work on an OLED/Mariko console running 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Target-specific applicability of the ns2jb chain.
entries.evidence: The author says the exploit was also tested on Switch 1, but does not identify the model or firmware. The published repository is Switch 2 only. No OLED/Mariko 23.0.1 test is documented.
entries.limitations: Do not assume that a Switch 1 test applies to the OLED or to 23.0.1. Independent reproduction or an author statement identifying the model and firmware is required.

entries.claim: A public exploit for CVE-2026-82079 is available.
entries.scope: Public exploit availability.
entries.evidence: The CVE record includes no exploit code and CISA ADP lists exploitation as none at the record update. Switchbrew links a HackerOne report for details, but no public packaged exploit was found in the reviewed sources.
entries.limitations: The HackerOne report may contain technical details and was not accessible in this review. The CVE record and CISA status are point-in-time observations, not proof that no exploit exists privately.

entries.claim: A public code-execution entry point through game save data or game cartridges exists on firmware 23.0.1.
entries.scope: Game save and game cartridge surfaces.
entries.evidence: The reviewed flaw list's Games section documents game-level infoleaks and anti-cheat issues, not a public game-save or cartridge code-execution chain on 23.0.1. No public chain was found.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding. Save editing and cartridge data manipulation are not code execution. The flaw list is not exhaustive.

entries.claim: The target console reports firmware 23.0.1 and serial prefix XTJ through PTP GetDeviceInfo, without opening a session.
entries.scope: Target console identity observation on 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: Ran `.venv/bin/python -m switch_usb_probe ptp-info --source ioreg --confirm` on 2026-10-26 with the console in Copy to PC via USB mode. The device enumerated as 057e:201d. DeviceInfo reported Manufacturer Nintendo, Model Nintendo Switch, Device version 23.0.1, serial prefix XTJ***, and 10 supported operations. Session opened: no. See research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-ptp.json.
entries.limitations: PTP DeviceInfo is what the console reports and can be spoofed by modified firmware. It does not establish the HEG-001 model number, OLED-versus-LCD hardware, no-modchip status, integrity, boot state, or exploitability.

entries.claim: GameShare sessions on the receiving system are handled by the splay system applet, which was introduced in system update 20.0.0.
entries.scope: Receiver-side implementation of GameShare.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's Splay Applet page identifies splay as the GameShare applet added with 20.0.0 and launched by qlaunch. The 20.0.0 change-log lists new title 0100000000001048 (splay) and describes GameShare as sharing software from a Switch 2 to nearby systems.
entries.limitations: This identifies the component and its introduction version. It does not describe a vulnerability or show that the applet can be subverted.

entries.claim: GameShare sends the receiving system a video stream plus setup metadata rather than a downloadable executable package.
entries.scope: Data flow from host to client.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew states that splay 'uses ldn to connect to the host' and that 'video streaming is used', and that during setup the host transfers the game NACP to the client along with JPEGs. Nintendo's GameShare FAQ states: 'By using streaming technology, it's possible to share the gameplay instantly without having to take time to transfer the software.'
entries.limitations: Public documentation describes streaming rather than a software transfer, but does not include a full protocol specification. The stronger claim that no executable code is ever sent is an inference, not a documented guarantee. Treat the exact wire format as UNKNOWN.

entries.claim: Only a Nintendo Switch 2 can host a GameShare session, and a Switch 1 or OLED system can only receive, and only over local wireless.
entries.scope: Host and transport prerequisites.
entries.evidence: Nintendo's GameShare FAQ states: 'Only Nintendo Switch 2 can share compatible games, and can share them online to Nintendo Switch 2 systems, or via local wireless communication to both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch systems', and 'A Nintendo Switch 2 system is required to host a GameShare session.' For internet sessions it states that only Switch 2 systems can join. The 20.0.0 change-log states the feature cannot be used between two Switch 1/OLED/Lite systems and that the Switch 2 must initiate.
entries.limitations: This bounds reachability. It does not mean a host cannot be spoofed by other means; it means Nintendo documents no such path and no public spoofing method was found.

entries.claim: The splay applet parses host-supplied data, including the game NACP and JPEG images during setup, and ECC signature verification is used for some of that data.
entries.scope: Receiver-side parsing of remote input.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew states that during setup the host transfers the game NACP to the client, that JPEGs are transferred as well, and that ECC signature verification is used in various functionality including verifying the AdvertiseData returned by Scan, with the public key selected via spl IsDevelopment.
entries.limitations: The wiki does not state which fields the signature covers or whether the stream itself is authenticated. JPEG decoding is handled by the separate jpegdec sysmodule, not necessarily inside splay. No parsing bug is documented.

entries.claim: The splay applet holds the StreamPlaySaveData filesystem permission (FsAccessFlag bit 47) and, on Switch 1 with 23.0.0 or later, access to news:c and stpl:sys.
entries.scope: Privileges available to the receiving applet.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's Splay Applet page states that with 23.0.0+ the Switch 1 applet has access to news:c and stpl:sys and that FS permission bit47 is set. The NPDM page names FsAccessFlag bit 47 StreamPlaySaveData. The 23.0.0 page records the same NPDM change for splay.
entries.limitations: A permission describes what the applet may reach if it is compromised; it is not a vulnerability and does not imply kernel or bootROM access.

entries.claim: A public vulnerability, proof of concept, or exploit for the GameShare protocol, the splay applet, or its NACP and JPEG handling was not found.
entries.scope: Public research status of the GameShare surface.
entries.evidence: The reviewed Switchbrew flaw list contains no entry for the splay applet, GameShare, StreamPlay, or jpegdec. No public write-up, advisory, or repository describing a GameShare or splay exploit was found in the reviewed sources.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding, not evidence that the surface is safe. Public flaw lists lag private research, and the absence of a listed bug says nothing about the actual robustness of the parser.

entries.claim: Even a complete compromise of the splay applet would yield applet-level userland code execution, not kernel, bootROM, or Atmosphère access.
entries.scope: Capability ceiling of the GameShare surface.
entries.evidence: The splay applet is an applet process whose documented NPDM grants a specific service list and filesystem permission bits, including StreamPlaySaveData. Nothing in the reviewed documentation gives it kernel capabilities, bootROM access, or the ability to launch unsigned boot code.
entries.limitations: This is an inference from the applet's privilege description, not the result of an exploit. A real chain could combine an applet primitive with a separate kernel vulnerability, which is exactly what is missing publicly.

entries.claim: The ns2jb chain combines a 32-bit integer overflow in the SmileBASIC interpreter with a path-normalization buffer overflow in the fs sysmodule, and the author says it was tested on Switch 1 but is not packaged for it.
entries.scope: Technical structure and platform status of the ns2jb chain.
entries.evidence: The author's write-up describes a 32-bit integer overflow in SmileBASIC's array removal check (position + count wraps), followed by a buffer overflow in fs Path::Normalize reached through the IFileSystem GetEntryType command using a path such as /..\, then arbitrary read/write and sysmodule code execution. It states the exploit 'has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven't gotten around to packaging it yet.' Ars Technica independently describes the SmileBASIC integer overflow.
entries.limitations: The Switch 1 test's model and firmware are not stated. Testing is not packaging, and the published repository is Switch 2 only. The fs bug's presence on Switch 1 23.0.1 is not independently documented.

entries.claim: The packaged ns2jb demo requires SmileBASIC 4.4.9, system software 23.0.1, a Node.js 22+ host, and more than 20 MiB free in the SmileBASIC save, and it installs no custom firmware or persistence.
entries.scope: Prerequisites and limits of the published package.
entries.evidence: The repository README states: 'You need SmileBASIC 4.4.9, system software 23.0.1, Node.js 22+ on macOS or Linux, and over 20 MiB free in the SmileBASIC save. The computer and console must be on the same reachable network.' It also states 'This demo does not install custom firmware or persistence' and 'Switch 2 only'.
entries.limitations: These are the packaged demo's requirements, not a general statement about the bug classes. The README does not give a Switch 1 procedure.

entries.claim: SmileBASIC 4 was delisted from the Nintendo eShop after the ns2jb release, which removes the entry point for anyone who does not already own it.
entries.scope: Availability of the documented ns2jb entry point.
entries.evidence: TwistedVoxel reported on 2026-10-22 that the UK eShop delisted SmileBASIC 4 and that it remained listed in the US, Canada, and Mexico at that time. TechSpot reported that it had disappeared from the US and European eShops. The ns2jb README pins the required version to 4.4.9.
entries.limitations: Store availability is region-dependent and changes over time. A previously purchased copy remains owned, and the demo or a physical copy may behave differently; neither is documented for this chain.

entries.claim: Gezine claims a Switch 1/2 userland exploit that is neither WebKit-based nor save-based, works offline across firmware versions, and remains unreleased with no public technical details.
entries.scope: A claimed but unpublished userland entry point.
entries.evidence: Wccftech quotes Gezine saying 'I created Switch 1/2 userland exploit that is not webkit or save exploit', that existing save-based userland exploits require online save transfer, and that this one works offline and across all firmware versions. The same article describes it as a userland starting point rather than a full jailbreak.
entries.limitations: No code, advisory, technical write-up, or independent reproduction was found. The claim does not identify the vulnerable component or the Switch 1 model and firmware. It cannot be treated as a method.

entries.claim: Gezine says SmileBASIC 4 is not strictly required for the Switch 2 chain, naming Artemis Engine and an undisclosed physical game cartridge as alternate triggers.
entries.scope: Alternate triggers for an unpublished chain.
entries.evidence: TwistedVoxel reports that Gezine said SmileBASIC 4 is not strictly necessary, that Artemis Engine could also be used, and that a physical game cartridge method may exist; Gezine did not disclose the cartridge and advised against buying Artemis Engine for this purpose.
entries.limitations: Secondary reporting of social-media posts with no technical detail, no package, and no reproduction. It does not establish that any alternate trigger works on Switch 1 23.0.1.

entries.claim: Caffeine is a warmboot exploit that let patched Erista consoles on 4.0.0-4.1.0 run full CFW without Fusée Gelée, which shows a software-only CFW path on a patched console is possible when the boot stage itself is exploitable.
entries.scope: Historical precedent for a warmboot-based CFW path on patched hardware.
entries.evidence: The Caffeine repository describes itself as 'an implementation of a warmboot exploit for Nintendo Switch running system software 4.1.0 and below (excluding 1.0.0)'. The Hacks Guide Wiki states that other patched Erista models may use the software method Caffeine if they run on versions 4.0.0 to 4.1.0, while Mariko-based models cannot be hacked via software.
entries.limitations: This is Erista only and more than six years old. It does not imply that a warmboot bug exists on Mariko or on 23.0.1; it only shows that the category is viable.

entries.claim: Warmboot is package1 section 0, and Mariko package1 is distributed in a signed and encrypted format, so a Mariko warmboot exploit would need a code bug in verified warmboot or TSEC code rather than a re-signed package.
entries.scope: Boot-chain structure relevant to stage 3.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew states that package1 section 0 contains the warmboot binary and section 2 the Secure Monitor, and that on Mariko the package is distributed in a custom, signed and encrypted format with an RSA-PSS signature at offset 0x10.
entries.limitations: The wiki documents the format, not the presence or absence of vulnerabilities. It does not prove that warmboot is hardened, only that replacing it requires defeating verification.

entries.claim: The ns2jb fs path-normalization bug is a privilege-escalation stage that requires a prior userland entry point, so it cannot function as an entry point by itself.
entries.scope: Stage position of the ns2jb fs bug.
entries.evidence: The write-up reaches the fs buffer overflow through an IFileSystem handle and the GetEntryType IPC command, after obtaining arbitrary read/write from the SmileBASIC interpreter overflow. The repository requires SmileBASIC 4.4.9 as the entry.
entries.limitations: This is a structural reading of the published write-up, not an independent audit. It is consistent with the repository's stated SmileBASIC requirement.

entries.claim: Artemis Engine games can chain-load Lua from an edited save file, but the public loader is documented for PS4 and Windows and does not provide native code or a documented Switch reproduction.
entries.scope: Save-based script loading as a candidate trigger.
entries.evidence: The ArtemisLuaLoader README states that most Artemis games automatically load save9999.dat on boot and that an edited save can chain-load inject.iet and then inject.lua. It lists Nintendo Switch among supported engine platforms, states testing was on Windows and PS4, and says the repository is unmaintained.
entries.limitations: Listing Switch as a supported engine platform is not evidence that the save chain-load works on Switch, and Lua execution inside a game is not native code execution. Copying a crafted save to a stock console is itself a constraint.

entries.claim: SmileBASIC 4 is distributed as Nintendo Switch download software, so there is no physical cartridge route to obtain the ns2jb entry point.
entries.scope: Acquisition of the documented ns2jb trigger.
entries.evidence: Nintendo's store listing classifies SmileBASIC 4 as Nintendo Switch download software. TwistedVoxel reported the UK eShop delisting on 2026-10-22.
entries.limitations: A demo is reported to exist in some regions, and its version and save capability are not documented for this chain. Availability is time-sensitive.

entries.claim: The documented capmtp PTP request surface carries only fixed-width integer parameters; the variable-length data in the protocol flows from the console to the host, not from the host to the console.
entries.scope: Shape of the host-to-console attack surface on capmtp.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew documents that only PTP operations 0x1001-0x100A are available. In those operations the request parameters are u32 values such as storage IDs, object handles, format codes, parent handles, offsets, and lengths. None is a string or a caller-supplied buffer. DeviceInfo, ObjectInfo, and object payloads are responses constructed by the console.
entries.limitations: This is derived from the PTP specification and the wiki's operation list, not from a capmtp binary. Undocumented vendor behavior remains possible, and fixed-width parameters do not preclude index-validation bugs or integer-overflow bugs.

entries.claim: On the target console, capmtp rejected invalid handle-table identifiers with documented PTP errors and stayed responsive across the tested cases.
entries.scope: Reproduced finding, one console and one run, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: With a session open, GetObjectHandles returned 0x2009 InvalidObjectHandle for an invalid storage ID with parent 0, and 0x200b InvalidObjectFormatCode for an invalid format code. GetObjectInfo returned 0x2009 for handles 0, 1, 0x7FFFFFFF, 0x80000000, and 0xFFFFFFFF. The storage/parent pair 0xFFFFFFFF/0xFFFFFFFF returned 0x2001 with 14 associations. See research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-ptp-boundary.json.
entries.limitations: Scoped to the tested identifiers. The 0xFFFFFFFF values have documented 'all' semantics. The object-read boundary family was not completed, and a later endpoint stall is unexplained and not attributed to this result.

entries.claim: On the target console, PTP GetObject (0x1009) returned 0x2006 ParameterNotSupported for every tested parameter set, so object data could not be read and offset/length validation was not exercised.
entries.scope: Reproduced finding, one console and one session, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: After discovering a non-empty object, GetObject was issued with offset and length at 0/0, 0/0x1000, size-1/0x1000, size/0x1000, size+1/0x1000, 0x7FFFFFFF/0x1000, 0x80000000/0x1000, 0xFFFFFFFF/0x1000, and 0/0x00100000. Every request returned 0x2006. A follow-up test with a full-object read (0/size) and a two-parameter form (handle/size) also returned 0x2006. GetObjectInfo for the same handle returned 0x2001 with a 166-byte dataset. See research/hardware-observations/2026-10-26-ptp-boundary.json.
entries.limitations: One session. The operation may be gated by an undocumented precondition, and GetThumb (0x100A) was not tested. The result does not prove that no other operation reads object data.

entries.claim: The target's WifiWebAuthApplet is reachable through a captive-portal DNS redirect and executes attacker-supplied JavaScript, and its User-Agent is a frozen compatibility token rather than a build identifier.
entries.scope: Reproduced finding, one console, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: With the console's primary DNS pointed at the host, the console queried ctest.cdn.nintendo.net, received the host address, and the WifiWebAuthApplet requested the portal page and posted the fingerprint JSON. The User-Agent was 'Mozilla/5.0 (Nintendo Switch; WifiWebAuthApplet) AppleWebKit/613.0 (KHTML, like Gecko) NF/6.0.3.31.11 NintendoBrowser/5.1.0.55481'. Public user-agent databases show the same AppleWebKit/613.0 token with NetFront 6.0.3.27.11, 6.0.3.30.3, and 7.0.3.11.3.
entries.limitations: One console and one applet. The WebApplet and account-login applets may differ and may enforce a URL whitelist. Reachability is not evidence of a vulnerability.

entries.claim: The observed browser environment supports ES2020 JavaScript features but reports WebAssembly unavailable and no WebGL, consistent with the documented absence of a JIT in the Switch browser.
entries.scope: Browser capability fingerprint.
entries.evidence: The page reported async functions, optional chaining, and BigInt as available, WebAssembly as unavailable, WebGL as null, hardwareConcurrency 4, and a 1280x720 screen at device pixel ratio 1. The arXiv paper states the Switch browser has no JIT.
entries.limitations: Feature detection bounds the engine generation but does not identify the build. WebAssembly may be disabled independently of JIT. WebGL absence may be a policy choice.

entries.claim: The target's WifiWebAuthApplet JavaScript engine is feature-bracketed to Safari 15.4-15.6 (WebKit 615.x, 2022): it supports features introduced in 15.4 and lacks features introduced in 16.0 and 16.4.
entries.scope: Feature-level engine generation, one console.
entries.evidence: The page reported Array.prototype.at, findLast, findLastIndex, structuredClone, Error cause, and RegExp match indices as present, all introduced in Safari 15.4. It reported Array.prototype.toSorted and toReversed as absent (Safari 16.0), and RegExp lookbehind as a SyntaxError (Safari 16.4). It also reported no Intl object, no WebAssembly, no Atomics, and no SharedArrayBuffer.
entries.limitations: Feature detection bounds the engine generation, not the security patch level. Nintendo can backport fixes without adding features, and the NetFront build number does change between firmware versions. One applet and one run.

entries.claim: Web-applets, including WifiWebAuthApplet, hold a broad userland IPC service list and SystemSaveData filesystem permission, so an applet compromise would be a meaningful userland foothold rather than an empty sandbox.
entries.scope: Documented NPDM privileges.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew lists access for all web-applets to services including acc:u1, appletAE, bsd:a, erpt:c, fatal:u, fsp-srv, hid, hid:sys, ldr:ro, mm:u, nifm:s, ns:web, nvdrv:a, pl:u, set:sys, sfdnsres, ssl, and vi:s, plus the SystemSaveData filesystem permission. The same page lists the optional svcMapPhysicalMemoryUnsafe code path added in 11.0.0.
entries.limitations: Service access is not a vulnerability, and applet privileges are still userland. Kernel or boot-stage execution would require a separate exploit.

entries.claim: CVE-2026-2441 is a Chromium/Blink CSS use-after-free and does not apply to the Switch's WebKit-based NetFront NX engine.
entries.scope: Applicability of a specific 2026 browser CVE.
entries.evidence: The NVD record names Google Chrome and the CSS component of Blink. Switchbrew identifies the Switch browser as NetFront NX, which is WebKit-based. A public PS4 test of the same CVE against NetFront NX also reported that the engine was not vulnerable, which is consistent with the different engine.
entries.limitations: This rules out one CVE, not the WebKit engine. It says nothing about WebKit-specific issues in the 15.4-15.6 bracket.

entries.claim: CVE-2022-32893 is the class of WebKit out-of-bounds write that would affect an unpatched Safari 15.4-15.6 engine, but no public proof of concept or technical analysis was found and Nintendo's backport status is unknown.
entries.scope: Candidate vulnerability class for the browser surface.
entries.evidence: The NVD record describes an out-of-bounds write in WebKit fixed in Safari 15.6.1 and reachable through crafted web content. The target engine is feature-bracketed to Safari 15.4-15.6. Searches found advisories and news coverage but no public proof of concept or exploitation write-up.
entries.limitations: The engine bracket is feature-level, not build-level; Nintendo may have backported the fix. No PoC was available to assess, and testing would be exploit execution. Even a successful exploit would be applet-level userland.

entries.claim: The target browser's JavaScript engine shows no measurable JIT warm-up, consistent with interpreter-only execution.
entries.scope: Timing measurement on the target browser applet, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: A 400,000-iteration integer loop took 40,39,40,40,39,40,40,39,40,40,39,40 ms across twelve consecutive runs. A shape-varying variant took 49 ms on eleven runs and 48 ms on one. There was no speed-up across runs and only a small monomorphic/polymorphic gap. WebAssembly remained unavailable. For comparison, the same loop shape under Node on the host collapsed from 6-7 ms to 0-1 ms after warm-up.
entries.limitations: Timing inference, not a direct engine inspection. A JIT could be disabled for this applet or not triggered within twelve runs, and CPU frequency scaling was not controlled. One console and one session.

entries.claim: The target captive-portal applet decodes PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP, and SVG images, including lossless WebP, so the image decoders are reachable with attacker-supplied files.
entries.scope: Reproduced finding, one console, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: scripts/fingerprint_formats.html loaded six 4x4 assets from the portal server. All six reported onload with correct naturalWidth/naturalHeight (GIF 1x1, others 4x4). The browser's Accept header advertised image/webp, image/png, and image/svg+xml. The WebP asset was produced with cwebp -lossless, so the lossless Huffman path was exercised. canvas and createImageBitmap were also available.
entries.limitations: Reachability is not vulnerability. The decoder implementation and its patch level are unknown. One console and one session.

entries.claim: The public CVE-2023-4863 reproducer is a valid trigger: against libwebp commit 7ba44f8 with AddressSanitizer it produces a heap-buffer-overflow in BuildHuffmanTable, while a non-ASAN build returns BITSTREAM_ERROR, so a non-ASAN no-crash is inconclusive.
entries.scope: Local reproduction of the trigger, not the console.
entries.evidence: Built libwebp commit 7ba44f80f3b94fc0138db159afea770ef06532a0 with -fsanitize=address. Running examples/dwebp on bad.webp and nso.webp produced 'ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow' with a WRITE of size 4 in BuildHuffmanTable (huffman_utils.c:194), called from ReadHuffmanCode (vp8l_dec.c:354). A non-ASAN libwebp 1.3.1 build returned 'Decoding failed. Status: 3(BITSTREAM_ERROR)' for both files.
entries.limitations: Local x86-64 build with a specific allocator, not the console's ARM build. The console may use a different libwebp version, a platform decoder, or a backported fix. Without ASAN, the overflow may be silent.

entries.claim: The target applet decoded both CVE-2023-4863 reproducer files to 1x1 images without a visible fault, while stock libwebp 1.2.4, 1.3.1, and 1.6.0 reject the same files with BITSTREAM_ERROR.
entries.scope: Console observation, 2026-10-26, plus local comparison builds.
entries.evidence: The portal served bad.webp (236 bytes, color_cache_bits=0) and nso.webp (350 bytes, color_cache_bits=6) to WifiWebAuthApplet. Both fired onload with naturalWidth/naturalHeight 1x1, and the page posted a 'done' marker. Locally, dwebp from libwebp 1.2.4, 1.3.1, and 1.6.0 returned 'Decoding failed. Status: 3(BITSTREAM_ERROR)' for both files. With ASAN on commit 7ba44f8, the same files produced a heap-buffer-overflow in BuildHuffmanTable.
entries.limitations: A non-ASAN silent overflow cannot be excluded. The applet's decoder implementation and version are unknown. One console and one run per file.

entries.claim: Sixty repeated decodes of the stronger CVE-2023-4863 reproducer completed without a visible fault; the applet stayed responsive and posted a completion marker.
entries.scope: Console observation, 2026-10-26.
entries.evidence: scripts/fingerprint_webp_stress.html decoded /assets/nso.webp sixty times with unique query strings to defeat the cache, posting an iteration marker before each decode. Iterations 0 through 59 all advanced and the page posted stage 'done' with count 60. No timeout, crash, or missing marker occurred.
entries.limitations: No AddressSanitizer. A silent out-of-bounds write cannot be excluded. The stress run exercised one allocation pattern; other heap layouts could behave differently. One console.

entries.claim: Stock libwebp releases 1.0.3 through 1.6.0 all reject the CVE-2023-4863 reproducers, while the target applet decodes them, so the applet's decoder is not stock libwebp and the CVE's applicability is unproven.
entries.scope: Local build sweep plus the console observation.
entries.evidence: Built libwebp 1.0.3, 1.1.0, 1.2.2, 1.2.3, 1.2.4, 1.3.1, and 1.6.0 and ran examples/dwebp on bad.webp and nso.webp. Every release returned BITSTREAM_ERROR for both files. The target applet decoded both to 1x1 images (E-067).
entries.limitations: The reproducers target a specific libwebp commit and may not generalize to every vulnerable build. The applet's decoder could still be a modified libwebp with different validation. This does not prove the applet is safe, only that the stock-libwebp trigger does not reproduce.

entries.claim: A crafted 64 MB FAT32 image with an MBR partition at 4 MiB mounts on the target console, which reports about 40 MB free.
entries.scope: Reproduced finding, one console, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: scripts/sdcard_lab.py built a FAT32 image with one 16-byte file and an MBR partition entry at LBA 8192. It was written to a sacrificial 31.9 GB microSD and inserted into the console. The console mounted it and reported approximately 40 MB free, which is less than the image's 63 MB because the console reserves space or writes its own structure.
entries.limitations: Mounting proves the parser accepts the container, not that any anomaly is handled safely. One console and one card.

entries.claim: The dir_cluster_oob image mounted and showed 40 MB free, but the crafted entry sits in the root directory and is not on a path the console walks during mount, so the out-of-range cluster was not necessarily dereferenced.
entries.scope: Mount observation and methodology, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The console mounted the image and reported the same capacity as the control. The image contained a single root-level TEST.TXT entry whose first cluster is 0x0FFFFFF0. Mounting validates the BPB and root directory; it does not require opening the file, so this result is not evidence that the bounds check is missing.
entries.limitations: The file was not opened, so the entry may never have been used. This is a negative on the test design, not on the driver.

entries.claim: Setting the Nintendo/Album directory entry's first cluster to 0x0FFFFFF0 causes the console's Album applet to hang and then report error 2802-9999.
entries.scope: Owner observation, one console, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The album_dir_oob image placed a Nintendo directory at cluster 3 and an Album directory entry whose first cluster is 0x0FFFFFF0. On insertion and opening the Album applet, the console hung and then displayed error code 2802-9999. The control image mounted normally.
entries.limitations: Whether the applet crashed or displayed a handled error is not yet established, and the console's recovery state is unconfirmed. 2802-9999 is a generic member of the album/SD error family. No crash report has been inspected.

entries.claim: After the out-of-range Album directory test the card contained console-created NINTENDO/Contents and NINTENDO/save entries with NAX0-magic files, and no crash report, indicating a handled applet failure rather than a system crash.
entries.scope: Card inspection after the album_dir_oob test, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: Mounted the card read-only from macOS. It contained NINTENDO/Contents/{registered,placehld,private,private1} and NINTENDO/save/{8000000000000000,8000000000000124}. The save entries begin with the ASCII magic 'NAX0'. No CrashReport directory or report file was present. The console remained responsive and the Album applet had displayed 2802-9999.
entries.limitations: The console may create these directories on any writable SD card as normal initialization. The files are encrypted and were not inspected further. Their presence is not evidence of a memory-safety bug.

entries.claim: The album_file_oob image mounts and the Album applet opens without error but shows no media from the card, so the crafted file entry was not exercised.
entries.scope: Owner observation, one console, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The image contained a valid Nintendo/Album directory with a valid OK.JPG and an out-of-range TEST.JPG. The Album applet opened normally and displayed no media from the microSD card, with no error code.
entries.limitations: Either the album's expected path or filename format differs from our 8.3 names, or the console replaced the crafted directory during mount. The bad entry was therefore not read.

entries.claim: The console's screenshot filename suffix is not the file's MD5, and the real JPEG contains a 14 KB APP1 Exif segment that our generated JPEG lacks.
entries.scope: File comparison on the card, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The real screenshot 2026102700452400-57B4628D2267231D57E0FC1078C0596D.jpg has MD5 ffa6936426b64d3c1689a3352915d80d, so the 32-hex suffix is not a content hash. Its JPEG segments begin with APP1 (0xE1, length 14258) and contain the Exif marker. Our generated 1280x720 JPEG begins with APP0 and has no Exif segment. Both are 1280x720, 72 dpi, sRGB.
entries.limitations: The album's behaviour with the real file present was not yet confirmed when this was recorded. Exif presence is a difference, not a proven filter.

entries.claim: A FAT32 image with sectors-per-cluster set to zero is rejected at mount with 'This microSD card cannot be used. Please format the microSD card.', with no hang or reboot.
entries.scope: Owner observation, one console, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The bpb_spc_zero image sets the BPB sectors-per-cluster byte to 0. On insertion the console displayed the format prompt instead of mounting. The console stayed responsive and did not reboot.
entries.limitations: The prompt is a handled validation path. It does not prove the driver never mishandles other BPB values.

entries.claim: The album lists the console's real screenshot placed at our crafted NINTENDO/ALBUM/2026/10/27 path and skips an out-of-range file entry in the same directory without error.
entries.scope: Owner observation, one console, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: The album_date_real image contained the console's exact JPEG bytes and filename at the crafted path, plus a second file whose first cluster is 0x0FFFFFF0. On opening the Album, the real screenshot appeared and no second item appeared. The console stayed responsive and reported no error.
entries.limitations: The skipped entry was not read, so this shows entry-level validation, not bounds checking inside the read path. One console.

entries.claim: Retail LDN encrypts advertisement and data frames; plaintext LDN is a development security mode, and the kinnay/LDN implementation supports a plaintext mode without deriving a WLAN data key.
entries.scope: Protocol and implementation documentation, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's LDN services page documents security mode 1 as product/encrypted, mode 2 as debug, and mode 3 as system debug/plaintext. The kinnay LDN protocol page states that levels 2 and 3 are only allowed during development and that the authentication challenge is always enabled for games but not for system titles. In the kinnay/LDN source, ConnectNetworkParam and CreateNetworkParam require a non-empty keys dictionary, but create_network derives a WLAN data key only when security_mode == SECURITY_MODE_PROD; for SECURITY_MODE_SYSTEM_DEBUG it passes wlan_key=None and AdvertisementFrame.build_advertisement selects the plaintext format. The package README requires Linux, monitor-mode action-frame support, CAP_NET_ADMIN/CAP_NET_RAW, and reports mt7921e as confirmed.
entries.limitations: Retail console acceptance of a plaintext network is untested. The fact that the host does not derive a key does not prove the console will accept the development-only mode. The authentication challenge is disabled for system titles but enabled for games.

entries.claim: Virtual game cards are gated by a Nintendo Account, an internet connection, local-wireless proximity, and a license; a PC cannot simply emulate a second console to join the flow.
entries.scope: Nintendo's virtual-game-card documentation, 2026-10-27.
entries.evidence: Nintendo's Virtual Game Card Guide states that a Nintendo Account can have up to two linked consoles that load virtual game cards, that both consoles must be connected to the internet for linking and loading, that local-wireless proximity is required for pairing and lending, and that lending is limited to Nintendo Account family group members. The game remains tied to the account and the license.
entries.limitations: This establishes the account/license and server gates, not the exact wire protocol. It does not prove that no implementation bug exists in the virtual-game-card code.

entries.claim: The 2026-10-28 Phase 2 plaintext LDN host run produced no JOIN and no room on the target, but the host's transmission is unconfirmed because the rtw88_8822bu driver reported 'failed to get tx report from firmware'.
entries.scope: Hardware observation, 2026-10-28. Owner report for the console screen; host log and dmesg for the host side.
entries.evidence: The host was started with --compat-no-active-ack for 2 seconds and then 30 seconds on channel 1 with title 0100a250097f0000, scene 0, security mode 3, and challenge disabled. Both runs ended with 'Host stopped.' and no JOIN. The console showed no room. dmesg reported 'failed to get tx report from firmware' after each run. A follow-up 60-second run on 2026-10-28 also produced no JOIN; three CoreWLAN scans from the Mac's built-in Wi-Fi did not show the 32-character SSID, but that check is invalid because the LDN host beacon uses a 32-byte null SSID and the network ID is carried in vendor action frames. dmesg logged a third TX-report failure. No valid independent receiver was used, so the host's frames may not have been on air. The sanitized record is research/hardware-observations/2026-10-28-ldn-phase2.json.
entries.limitations: The console screen is an owner report, not an automated capture. The adapter's TX path is unconfirmed. The 60-second CoreWLAN scan could not see the null-SSID beacon and is not a valid transmission check. One game and three runs were tested. The result does not show whether retail 23.0.1 would accept security mode 3 if the host transmitted.

entries.claim: The owner-provided prod.keys decrypt the Phase 1 Dragon Ball FighterZ LDN advertisement, confirming that the retail room uses security mode 1 (product/encrypted) with the challenge enabled.
entries.scope: Hardware observation and local decryption, 2026-10-28. The keys and firmware dump are owner-provided and excluded from version control.
entries.evidence: The owner supplied a prod.keys file and a firmware 23.0.1 dump from their own modded Switch. Both are local-only and ignored by git. Using the kinnay/LDN KeyDerivation with key-derivation protocol 1 and the captured Phase 1 pcap, the advertisement decrypted and its SHA-256 validated. The decrypted payload reports security mode 1 (prod), challenge present, channel 1, band 2.4 GHz, max_participants 2, num_participants 1, app_version 26, and 4 bytes of application data. The title ID and scene ID match the plaintext header (0100a250097f0000, 0). The sanitized record is research/hardware-observations/2026-10-28-ldn-phase1.json.
entries.limitations: The keys are from the owner's other modded Switch, not from the target. The target remains unmodified. The decryption proves key compatibility and the room's security mode; it does not prove that the PC can transmit or join. The firmware dump's version is owner-reported and folder-named 23.0.1; it was not independently verified with a firmware tool. SSID, MAC addresses, server random, application data, and key material are not recorded.

entries.claim: The owner supplied a local 23.0.1 firmware dump and a prod.keys file from their own modded Switch; both are excluded from version control and available for read-only analysis.
entries.scope: Local artifact inventory, 2026-10-28. The target console remains unmodified.
entries.evidence: Firmware/Firmware.23.0.1 contains 238 files (117 program/data NCAs and 121 cnmt.nca files) and is about 325 MB. Firmware/prod.keys.txt contains 222 well-formed keys, including master_key_00 through master_key_14, aes_kek_generation_source, and aes_key_generation_source. .gitignore excludes Firmware/, Firmware.*/, and prod.keys*; git check-ignore confirms both paths are ignored. The keys decrypt the Phase 1 LDN advertisement (E-081). No hactool or nxdump is installed, so package1 and the NCAs have not been extracted or independently verified.
entries.limitations: The dump's version is owner-reported and folder-named 23.0.1; it was not verified with a firmware tool. The keys are from the owner's other modded Switch, not from the target. Artifact contents, hashes, and decrypted modules must remain local and must never be committed, published, or shared.

entries.claim: The owner's 23.0.1 firmware dump is an NCA-only set whose ldn sysmodule is title 0100000000000018, version 0x5c0004b0; the supplied keys decrypt its metadata but not the NCA key generation needed to decrypt the program content.
entries.scope: Read-only NCA header and metadata parsing of the owner's local firmware dump, 2026-10-29. No program NCA content was decrypted.
entries.evidence: The dump contains 238 NCA files and no package1 or other non-NCA files. All 238 NCA headers decrypted as valid NCA3 with the owner's header_key. Content types: 76 program, 121 meta, 38 data, 3 public data. Key-generation counts: 126 at 0x00, 2 at 0x07, 1 at 0x0b, 1 at 0x10, 3 at 0x14, 1 at 0x15, 8 at 0x16, and 96 at 0x17. The ldn NCA is 755bcf33085ed666cbbcf34de83d1cb0.nca, title 0100000000000018, a 556,544-byte program NCA with key generation 0x17 and a 556,032-byte AES-CTR PartitionFS section 0. The ldn meta NCA 5bc39286ff59b4bd3abc2bbca467e86c.cnmt.nca decrypted with key_area_key_application_00 and reports title version 0x5c0004b0 (1543505072), content type SystemProgram, and the NCA SHA-256 755bcf33085ed666cbbcf34de83d1cb0f7ceaa0ebf7a106dfa54a2d54b193072, which matches the local NCA file. Key generation 0x17 requires key_area_key_application_16; the prod.keys file contains key_area_key_application_00 through _14 only. The sanitized record is research/hardware-observations/2026-10-29-firmware-inventory.json.
entries.limitations: The dump's version is owner-reported and folder-named 23.0.1; it was not independently verified. The title-ID mapping for ldn comes from a community list, though the title ID and version are read from the decrypted CNMT. The program NCA content was not decrypted, so this does not analyze the parser. Package1 is absent, so the warmboot direction cannot use this dump.

entries.claim: In upstream mac80211, NL80211_CMD_FRAME can transmit an AP beacon through the normal TX path, but a non-public action frame on an AP interface requires a station entry; a broadcast destination is not a station, so an LDN vendor action frame cannot be broadcast from an AP interface through this path.
entries.scope: Source-level analysis of upstream Linux mac80211/nl80211 on 2026-10-29. Not tested on the running OrbStack kernel or the adapter.
entries.evidence: cfg80211_mgmt_tx_check requires the BSSID of a non-public action frame on an AP interface to equal the AP address. ieee80211_mgmt_tx then looks up a station for the frame's destination address and returns -ENOLINK if none exists. NL80211_ATTR_FRAME_NO_STA sets params.no_sta, but the upstream code still returns -ENOLINK for a non-public action frame with no station. Beacon frames skip the action-category and station checks, and the AP TX frame-type mask includes beacon (0x80), so a beacon can be sent through NL80211_CMD_FRAME. The source is the upstream mac80211 offchannel.c and net/wireless/nl80211.c, reviewed 2026-10-29.
entries.limitations: The running kernel is 7.2.12-orbstack-00394-gbecdd6130068, not upstream master. A driver or kernel patch could differ. The source analysis does not show whether a unicast vendor action frame to a station entry is accepted by the console's LDN parser. It also does not test the adapter's AP-mode NL80211_CMD_FRAME path.

entries.claim: On the AP interface, NL80211_CMD_CONTROL_PORT_FRAME with ethertype 0x88B7 is rejected with EINVAL, while the same command with EAPOL ethertype 0x888E is accepted. An AF_PACKET raw Ethernet frame with ethertype 0x88B7 is transmitted as a protected CCMP data frame with KeyID 0 when the station is authorized and the pairwise key is installed; without station authorization, the same raw 0x88B7 frame is accepted by the socket but not transmitted.
entries.scope: Local AP-mode control on 2026-10-29 with a fake station, a synthetic CCMP key, the rtw88_8822bu AP interface on channel 1, and the same-phy mon-ldn monitor vif. No console was involved.
entries.evidence: The AP interface reached AP-ENABLED with the room's SSID and the LDN RSN IE. A fake station (`02:00:00:00:00:01`) was added with AID 1, a synthetic pairwise CCMP key was installed, and a control-port frame with ethertype 0x88B7 returned `[Errno 22] Invalid argument`; the same command with ethertype 0x888E was accepted and the monitor captured it as a protected data frame with KeyID 0. A raw AF_PACKET send of an Ethernet frame with ethertype 0x88B7 returned success (27 bytes) but the monitor saw only the 0x888E frame, because the fake station was not authorized. The test then authorized the station with NL80211_CMD_SET_STATION (`NL80211_ATTR_STA_FLAGS2` mask/set 0x2 and the nested `NL80211_STA_FLAG_AUTHORIZED` flag), installed the same pairwise key, and sent both raw frames. The monitor captured two protected data frames to the fake station with IV 1 and IV 2 and KeyID 0; the 0x88B7 frame was the second. This is the response path the harness uses after association, because the control-port command cannot carry the LDN ethertype on this driver.
entries.limitations: The station was synthetic and no console received the frames. The monitor capture is on the same phy and may include loopback; it shows the AP's protected TX frames, not independent RF reception. The test used one adapter, driver, kernel, and channel. The exact authorization flag combination was redundant (flags2 and nested flags were both set), so the test does not isolate which encoding is required; it only shows that an authorized station with an installed pairwise key transmits the raw 0x88B7 frame. The raw path requires the station to be authorized and the pairwise key to be installed before the send. The host BSSID, interface, and fake station MAC are local test values; the console MAC and room SSID are not used in this record.

The monitor pcap (`/tmp/ap-ldn-monitor.pcap`, local-only, 229,429 bytes) contains 70 unicast LDN action frames to the console, one console probe request with a 32-byte non-zero SSID, one probe response to the console with a 32-byte non-zero SSID plus the RSN and extended-capabilities IEs, and exactly one console data frame: a 28-byte null-data frame (subtype 4, no payload, unprotected, flags=0x01). There is no console data payload frame and no 0x88B7 frame. The AP raw socket saw one 20-byte frame with ethertype `0x0006` and payload `0001af810100`; it is probably a non-LDN control or null frame. The owner observed `2203-0066` after a few seconds and the game popup `unable to join the room`; the console returned to the game normally. The sanitized record is research/hardware-observations/2026-10-29-ap-mode-ldn-join-third.json.
entries.limitations: The run was interrupted at about eight seconds, so the full 90-second window was not observed; the console had already disassociated by then. No independent receiver captured the AP's transmissions; the monitor pcap is on the same phy and may include loopback. The console reaction is owner-reported and was not instrumented. No 0x88B7 request was observed, so the run cannot distinguish a console abort before the request from a receive-path miss. The disassociation cause is not proven; the leading remaining host-side difference is that hostapd sends a zero-length beacon SSID while the ldn MonitorAP sends 32 zero bytes. One adapter, driver, kernel, and channel. The host BSSID, interface, console MAC, room SSID, application data, keys, and pcap are redacted or local-only.

entries.claim: A read-only review of the public GameShare/splay documentation and the 23.0.0/23.0.1 changelogs found no public vulnerability, proof of concept, or exploit for splay, the GameShare protocol, or its NACP/JPEG handling. 23.0.0 updated splay's NPDM (FsAccessFlag bit 47, news:c, stpl:sys, KernelVersion 27.1) and RomFS (lyt, message, sound), but the changelog records no splay security fix; 23.0.1 updated only sdb and did not update splay.
entries.scope: Public-source review on 2026-10-29 of Switchbrew's Splay Applet, 20.0.0, 23.0.0, 23.0.1, and Switch System Flaws pages plus Nintendo's GameShare FAQ. No active testing and no GameShare host were used.
entries.evidence: Switchbrew's 23.0.0 page lists splay among the updated applets and records only NPDM and RomFS changes: Fac.FsAccessFlag bit 47 set (0x0000800000000000), service access added news:c and stpl:sys, KernelCap KernelVersion 9.1 -> 27.1, and RomFS updates under /lyt/, /message/, and /sound/splay_action.bksnd. It does not list a splay security fix. The 23.0.1 page lists only sdb among updated sysmodules, with a SystemVersion RomFS update and a stability change-log entry; splay is not listed. The Switch System Flaws page contains no splay, GameShare, StreamPlay, or jpegdec entry. No public advisory, write-up, or repository describing a splay or GameShare exploit was found in the reviewed sources. The 20.0.0 page and Nintendo FAQ still identify splay as the receiver-side GameShare applet.
entries.limitations: This is an absence-of-documented-method finding in the reviewed sources, not proof that splay is safe. The 23.0.1 security-flaw field is an unfilled placeholder, and changelogs can omit security fixes. The protocol is not publicly specified, and no public source documents the exact ECC coverage, NACP/JPEG parsing, or stream format. No code or console test was performed.

entries.claim: In the owner's local 23.0.1 dump, the 76 program NCAs split by key generation into 0x07:1, 0x15:1, 0x16:7, and 0x17:67. The only 0x15 program is miiEdit (0100000000001009), which decrypts with key_area_key_application_14 and confirms the local NCA decryption path. splay's program NCA is key generation 0x17 and remains encrypted, but its key-generation-0x00 meta NCA is readable and its CNMT matches the program NCA.
entries.scope: Read-only local parsing of the owner's NCA dump and keys on 2026-10-29. Header decryption used header_key; the miiEdit section was decrypted with key_area_key_application_14; the splay meta CNMT was decrypted with key_area_key_application_00. No content was published and no console was involved.
entries.evidence: All 238 NCA headers parsed. Program NCAs: 76; key-generation counts 0x07:1 (flog, 01008bb00013c000), 0x15:1 (miiEdit, 0100000000001009, c5d032046782d4bd6fc4b5c012a4e110.nca, 16,103,424 bytes, crypto type 2), 0x16:7, and 0x17:67. The miiEdit section-0 master hash verified with key_area_key_application_14, and its ExeFS PFS0 contains main, main.npdm, rtld, and sdk; the NPDM name is miiEdit. It is a Mii editor applet, not a remote-input surface. splay's program NCA is b837233731cc2c6b3bc384489be7d46a.nca, 6,722,560 bytes, key generation 0x17, crypto type 2; its meta NCA e481ece5d922f9a3776493f891fa0ef9.cnmt.nca is 3,584 bytes at key generation 0x00 and crypto type 0. The splay CNMT reports title 0100000000001048, version 0x5c0004b0, ContentMetaType 1 (SystemProgram), one Program content entry with content ID b837233731cc2c6b3bc384489be7d46a and size 0x669400 (6,722,560); the CNMT SHA-256 matches the local program NCA exactly. key_area_key_application_16 is absent, so the splay program key area and section remain encrypted.
entries.limitations: The dump's version is owner-reported and folder-named 23.0.1. Title-name mappings for flog, miiEdit, and splay come from community lists; the title IDs, versions, sizes, and key generations are read from the local headers and CNMT. The miiEdit decryption proves the local NCA path works for key generation 0x15, but it does not provide the missing 0x17 key. No splay code was decrypted or analyzed.

entries.claim: A host-only D10 Phase 0 baseline on 2026-10-29 brought up an open AP (TX10LED-NET) and a WPA2-PSK/CCMP AP (TX10LED-WPA2) on the TP-Link Archer T3U Plus in AP mode. Both SSIDs were visible from an independent macOS CoreWLAN scan at -34 dBm on channel 1. dnsmasq 2.92, radvd 2.20, OpenSSL 3.5.5, Scapy 2.8.0, and tcpdump 4.99.6 passed start/stop checks. A same-phy monitor interface was created while the AP ran but captured zero frames from the AP's BSSID, so management-frame attribution must use hostapd debug logs and the independent scan.
entries.scope: Host-only Phase 0 of docs/WIFI-NETWORK-TEST-PLAN.md on 2026-10-29. The console was not connected, powered on for this test, or otherwise involved. The test transmitted ordinary AP beacons and probe responses only; no malformed frame, DHCP/DNS/IPv6/TLS response, or console-directed data was sent.
entries.evidence: The adapter enumerated as 2357:0138 with rtw88_8822bu firmware 30.20.0. hostapd 2.11 reached AP-ENABLED on channel 1 (2412 MHz) for both configurations; the WPA2 log records wpa_version=0x2, PSK derivation, and group-key installation. The macOS CoreWLAN wildcard scan saw TX10LED-NET at -34 dBm on channel 1 on the third attempt and TX10LED-WPA2 at -34 dBm on the second attempt, then at -35 dBm during a capture-time scan; the returned BSSIDs were nil. A same-phy monitor interface was added while the AP ran and tcpdump captured 80 ambient channel-1 frames, but zero frames with the adapter BSSID and zero TX10LED frames; the hostapd -dd log recorded probe requests and probe responses, including one at -35 dBm. dnsmasq bound DHCP port 67 and DNS port 53 on 192.168.77.1 and stopped cleanly; radvd started and stopped cleanly with 2001:db8:77::1/64 and IPv6 forwarding, which was restored; OpenSSL s_server started and stopped on 127.0.0.1:8443; Scapy listed the AP interface; tcpdump captured 3 packets on eth0. The adapter was restored to managed mode and all test addresses were removed.
entries.limitations: One adapter, one driver, one kernel, and channel 1 only. macOS returned nil BSSIDs for every network, so only SSID, RSSI, and channel were usable. The same-phy monitor did not see the AP's own frames and is not a valid attribution path for injected frames on this driver. Phase 0 did not test client association, DHCP, DNS, IPv6, or TLS with a console. The adapter required a USB detach/attach and module reload after an initial -110 register-write failure. This is feasibility evidence, not a parser or vulnerability result.

entries.claim: On 2026-10-29 the target console associated to TX10LED-NET (open) and TX10LED-WPA2 (WPA2-PSK/CCMP), completed the WPA2 pairwise handshake, obtained DHCP lease 192.168.77.94, queried ctest.cdn.nintendo.net, and failed at the connect-to-internet step with 2110-3128 because the test AP had no NAT or upstream route. No malformed frames were sent.
entries.scope: D10 Phase 1 on 2026-10-29. The owner added the two test SSIDs, connected the console, and ran Test Connection once per SSID. The test AP served only DHCP and DNS; it had no NAT or internet forwarding. No malformed 802.11, DHCP, DNS, IPv6, or TLS data was sent.
entries.evidence: Open state: hostapd logged open-system authentication, association with AID 1, and AP-STA-CONNECTED. dnsmasq logged DHCPOFFER/DHCPREQUEST/DHCPACK for 192.168.77.94 with a 12-hour lease, router 192.168.77.1, and DNS server 192.168.77.1. The console queried ctest.cdn.nintendo.net; dnsmasq resolved it through CNAMEs ctest.cdn.nintendo.net.akamaized.net and a1456.g1.akamai.net to 2.19.126.212 and 2.19.126.222. The AP-interface pcap shows a TCP SYN from 192.168.77.94 to 2.19.126.212:80. Test Connection reported 2110-3128 at the connect-to-internet step. WPA2 state: hostapd logged 802.11 authentication, association with AID 1, 1/4 and 3/4 EAPOL-Key messages, 'pairwise key handshake completed (RSN)', authorized=1, and AP-STA-CONNECTED. dnsmasq again logged DHCP for 192.168.77.94 and the same ctest.cdn.nintendo.net query; Test Connection again reported 2110-3128. The console also sent IPv6 router solicitations to ff02::2; no RA was offered. The AP, DHCP/DNS server, and capture were stopped, the test address was removed, and the adapter was restored to managed mode.
entries.limitations: The absence of NAT explains the internet-step failure, so this baseline did not reach the TLS endpoint. The console's error code is recorded as displayed and its internal cause was not decoded. EAPOL frames were not visible on the AP interface because hostapd consumed them; the handshake evidence is the hostapd debug log. One console, one adapter, and channel 1 only. The two test networks remain saved on the console until the owner removes them. This is a reachability baseline, not a parser or vulnerability result.
